column3: Giant pandas live among bamboo groves just outside Chengdu, where you can watch them munch, climb and nap. Early morning is when they are most active.
Three parallel lanes of old courtyard houses from the Qing dynasty, now filled with teahouses, snack shops and small galleries.
A lantern-lit old street next to the Wuhou Shrine, with snack stalls, craft shops and tea houses in the style of the Three Kingdoms.
A temple for Zhuge Liang, the brilliant strategist of the Three Kingdoms, which is also a shrine for his lord Liu Bei, set among cypress trees.
The simple home where the Tang poet Du Fu lived for four years, now a peaceful garden with bamboo, ponds and a museum.
An irrigation system begun around 256 BC that still waters the Chengdu plain. It splits a river without a dam, and still works after more than 2,000 years.
A Taoist mountain covered in green forest and temples, one of the birthplaces of Taoism, and quiet and cool in summer.
Chengdu's big pedestrian shopping street, with department stores and fashion shops, and a lively place in the evening.
A well-known teahouse in People's Park, where people sit in bamboo chairs, sip tea and chat all afternoon, and ear cleaners go from table to table.
Soft tofu and minced beef in a bright red, hot and numbing sauce of chili bean paste and Sichuan pepper. It was created in Chengdu in the 19th century.
Pork belly boiled, sliced and stir-fried with chili bean paste and leeks. It is often called the soul of Sichuan cooking.
Diced chicken with peanuts and dried chilies, in a sweet, sour and spicy sauce, said to be named after a Qing official.
Cold sliced beef and beef offal in a spicy chili-oil sauce with peanuts and herbs, with an old Chengdu street-food story.
Shredded pork with wood-ear mushrooms in a sweet, sour and spicy sauce that was originally used for fish. There is no fish in it.
Sichuan wontons, whose name means folded hands, are served in broth or in a red chili-oil sauce.
Chewy glutinous rice balls with a sweet sesame or bean filling, served in a warm broth, a century-old Chengdu snack.
A thin, soft, pan-fried pancake folded around a sweet or savory filling, a Chengdu street snack.
Dumplings in a sweet and spicy red-oil sauce, from a shop that has been selling them for around 100 years.
Thick noodles in a sweet and savory sauce of soy, garlic and sesame, a classic Chengdu snack.
Skewers dipped into a bubbling, spicy pot. You pay by counting the empty sticks at the end of the meal.
Tea served in a bowl with a lid and a saucer, a fixture of Chengdu teahouses, where you can sit for hours with refills.
Performers in Sichuan opera swap painted masks in the blink of an eye, with a wave of a fan or a sweep of a cloak, and their secrets are closely guarded.
Sichuan embroidery uses very fine stitches and silk threads, often to depict pandas, flowers and fish, one of the four great styles of Chinese embroidery.
A brocade woven in Chengdu since ancient times and traded along the Silk Road, famed for its rich colors and patterns.
A fermented paste of broad beans and chili from Pixian, the essential base of Sichuan cooking, deep red and savory.
Noodles with chili oil, minced pork and preserved vegetables. The name comes from vendors who carried the noodles on a shoulder pole.
Rabbit pieces cooked dry with chilies and spices, then eaten cold. A famous snack from Zigong.
Giant lantern figures, such as dinosaurs and dragons, light up Zigong around the Spring Festival, in one of the biggest lantern shows in China.
A 71-meter Buddha carved into a cliff where three rivers meet. The carving took about 90 years in the Tang dynasty, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
One of China's four sacred Buddhist mountains, with temples, misty forests and mischievous monkeys on the way up.
The top of Mount Emei, where people come for sunrises, a sea of clouds and a gilded temple with a big golden statue.
Cold shredded chicken in a sesame and chili sauce. The name comes from beating the cooked chicken with a stick to make it tender.
Chicken and other skewered food that is served cold in a bowl of spicy red oil, a Leshan snack.
A peppery beef and offal soup, served with vegetables and noodles, a Leshan specialty.
Tofu from the Xiba district fried and grilled until crisp outside and soft inside, and eaten with a dipping sauce.
A Bronze Age site where giant bronze masks with bulging eyes and a golden mask were found, from a mysterious ancient kingdom that left no writing.
Colorful woodblock prints from Mianzhu, hung on doors at the Spring Festival to bring luck.
A well-known Sichuan baijiu, made in Mianzhu with a long history that goes back to the Tang dynasty.
Rice noodles in a rich, spicy beef broth, a Mianyang breakfast favorite.
Steamed noodles served cool with chili oil, vinegar and garlic, a refreshing dish from Guangyuan.
A well-preserved old town on a bend of the Jialing River, with Tang and Song layout, courtyard houses, and a gate tower.
Spiced, air-dried beef from Langzhong, named after the Three Kingdoms general Zhang Fei.
Oily, spicy noodles that were said to burn if you light them, from Yibin's streets.
Thinly sliced boiled pork rolled around a garlic and chili sauce, a classic of Lizhuang.
A famous baijiu made from five grains in Yibin, which is one of the most valued liquors in China.
A cold-water fish from the rivers of Ya'an, cooked in a spicy broth, a local delicacy.
The spice that makes your mouth tingle. Hanyuan County is famous for it, and cooks across Sichuan use it.
A glacier that flows down into a forest, with hot springs nearby, a place where ice meets greenery.
Three snow peaks in a remote Tibetan valley, with blue lakes and wide meadows, often called the last Shangri-La.
Tea churned with yak butter and salt, a daily Tibetan drink that keeps people warm at altitude.
Roasted barley flour mixed with butter tea and kneaded by hand, a Tibetan staple.
Turquoise lakes, terraced waterfalls and forests in a valley of Tibetan villages. The name means Nine Village Valley, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Terraced pools of golden limestone that wind down a valley, said to look like a yellow dragon, and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A range of snowy peaks with grasslands and glacier valleys, nicknamed the Oriental Alps.
An old frontier town with walls and gates, a base for horse treks into the mountains.
A Tibetan drink brewed from highland barley, slightly sweet and sour, served at festivals.
The Yi people's festival of fire, wrestling and dancing, with torches carried through the fields at night, to drive away evil.
Wooden bowls and cups painted in red, black and yellow in traditional Yi patterns, a craft of the Liangshan area.
Sweet mangoes grown in the warm, dry valleys of Panzhihua, which ripen early in the year.
A rich braised pork knuckle named for the poet Su Dongpo, who was born in Meishan.
Beef sliced so thin you could see a lamp through it, then dried and spiced, a Dazhou specialty.
The central pedestrian district of Chongqing, around a tall monument, with shops and restaurants.
A cliffside block of stilted buildings that glows at night above the Jialing River, which looks like a scene from a fantasy film.
An old river port of stone lanes, teahouses and snack stalls, with a taste of old Chongqing.
A light-rail line that runs straight through an apartment block, which has become a symbol of Chongqing's vertical city.
A cable car across the Yangtze, which gives views of the city's skyline and the river below.
A bubbling pot of beef tallow, chilies and Sichuan pepper, in which you cook meat, tripe and vegetables. This fiery meal is the pride of Chongqing.
A spicy, numbing bowl of noodles that many locals eat for breakfast, with a rich, oily sauce.
Glass noodles made of sweet potato starch in a sour and spicy broth with peanuts and chili oil.
Duck blood, tripe and other ingredients simmered in a very spicy broth, a Chongqing classic.
Fish slices poached in a layer of hot chili oil, with bean sprouts. It is said to have started in Chongqing.
Fish in a sour and peppery broth with pickled mustard greens, a favorite family dish.
Chicken pieces buried in a heap of dried chilies, from Gele Mountain, where you hunt for the pieces.
Soft tofu eaten with rice and a spicy dipping sauce, a simple, filling Chongqing meal.
Sticky rice cakes rolled in brown sugar and soy flour, a sweet snack.
Bold, home-style dishes that began in small riverside restaurants, and are cooked with strong flavors.
Work songs sung by boat trackers on the upper Yangtze, with a rhythm that matched the hauling of boats.
A temple on a hill at the head of the Three Gorges, famous in poems by Li Bai and Du Fu.
The first and shortest of the Three Gorges, with steep cliffs on both sides of the river.
Sweet navel oranges grown on the hills above the Yangtze, harvested in winter.
Crunchy, sweet plums that grow on the slopes of Wushan, picked in early summer.
A salty, spicy pickle made from mustard tuber, which is a famous export of Fuling, enjoyed with congee.
Crisp roast goose from Rongchang, a local specialty, with juicy meat.
A hill covered in temples and statues about the afterlife, a place of folklore and legends.
Chicken chopped small and cooked with a heap of chilies and Sichuan pepper, a spicy specialty of Fengdu.
A wooden temple tower built up the side of a rock beside the Yangtze, like a multi-story pagoda.
A savory fermented tofu with a long local history, used to flavor rice and vegetables.
A bright, numbing green Sichuan pepper grown around Jiangjin, with a fresh fragrance.
Fish grilled whole, then simmered in a spicy sauce with vegetables, a famed dish of Wanzhou.
